bib.title: AutoGym: Blueprint-First Generation of Verifiable Agent Gyms

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AutoGym: Blueprint-First Generation of Verifiable Agent Gyms", Aarati Andrea Noronha, Kavya Ravikumar, Carly Xiaoyu Lin (Amazon AGI). Preprint, arXiv:2609.22592v1 [cs.AI], dated 18 Sep 2026 (p1). First author Noronha, September 2026, no venue.
COVERAGE: 28 of 28 pages, 89,126 chars, all read. That covers body, limits, appendices A-H (parameters, rubric, verifier, two task samples, cost, GRPO study, prompt templates). Pages 10-13 are references, skimmed. Pages 23-28 are prompt templates, read in part. Figure 2 is a plot with no numbers in the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Parameters steer difficulty (note 06, simulated/synthetic environments). Moving only topology weights, obfuscation and distractor budget from C1 to C2 raises Opus 4.6 "hard" tasks from 10% to 39%.
 number: C1 10.0/34.7/55.3 (hard/med/easy), N=297; C2 39.0/10.0/51.0, N=280
 setup: productivity gym, 7 tools, generator Claude Sonnet 4.6, 8 rollouts per task, success = verifier score 1; hard <0.30, easy >=0.80
 quote: "Under configuration C2, where the same parameters are pushed toward the mid-to-hard range, 39% of generated tasks fall in the hard band." (p7)
2. Baselines (Table 1, p7). For Opus 4.6, hard/med/easy is 21.5/12.4/66.1 on human expert-authored (N=300) and 4.0/6.0/90.0 on Agent World Model (N=217, kept from 300 after manual review). For gpt-oss-120b: expert 40/20/40, AWM 9/13/78, C1 33.4/40.5/26.1, C2 70/17/13. The authors say a uniformly easy gym gives no learning signal and a uniformly hard one gives sparse reward.
3. Cross-model discrimination (note 06). On C2, 70% of tasks are hard for gpt-oss-120b against 39% for Opus 4.6. The authors read this as the tasks measuring capability rather than noise.
 quote: "For Claude Opus 4.6, 61% of tasks fall in the medium or easy bands. For gpt-oss-120b, only 30% do, with 70% classified as hard." (p8)
4. Failure-driven curriculum (note 06, note 07). Trajectories from gpt-oss-120b showed temporal reasoning as a failure mode. The pipeline produced a 92-task gym kept from 100 candidates.
 number: Opus 4.6 6.5/4.3/89.2; gpt-oss-120b 20.7/20.6/58.7 (Table 4, p9). All 10 tasks outside Opus's easy band are hard for gpt-oss, plus 9 more hard for gpt-oss alone; none is harder for Opus.
 quote: "No task is harder for the frontier model than for the weaker one." (p8)
 The 10 non-easy tasks were manually inspected and judged well-formed. The text states 89.1% easy while Table 4 shows 89.2%, a small inconsistency.
5. Repair filters defective tasks (notes 06 and 07, verifier reliability). Yield after repair was 84.9% for C1 (297 of 350), 80.0% for C2 (280 of 350), 92% for temporal (92 of 100) and 86% overall in the six-domain 600-task suite (p7, App F). Table 2 shows C2 hard share falling from 57.0% before repair to 39.0% after.
 quote: "showing how validation removes cases whose apparent difficulty arises from environment, ground-truth, or verifier defects rather than agent capability." (p8)
 Repair was three iterations. It is triggered only by environment or verifier defects, never by agent failure (p6).
6. Cost (note 10, engineering RL systems). Per task, AutoGym costs $2-5 at mid-tier pricing and $3-8 at frontier pricing, against $500-1000 for expert authoring (Table 8). A 50-task gym at 20-way parallelism costs $100-150 mid-tier or $150-200 frontier, taking 54 minutes against 2-4 weeks for experts (Table 9). Expert cost is an estimate. The human validation study is excluded from AutoGym's cost.
 quote: "AutoGym achieves two orders of magnitude cost reduction and roughly 100× wall-clock speedup." (p22)
7. RL training evidence is thin (note 10). A 600-task instruction-following gym, one 8B checkpoint, GRPO for 500 steps. The reward rises steadily (Fig 2, p22), but no numbers, no held-out evaluation and no baseline are given. The authors concede "limited to a single 8B model over 500 GRPO steps" (p9).
8. LLM certification audit (7 rubric dimensions, 0-100, judge blind to generation). Productivity gym: scope 92.7, groundedness 91.4, scalability 90.0, task realism 89.0, environment realism 86.0, diversity 80.0, interface realism 78.0 (Table 3). Temporal gym: 96.7, 93.4, 97.0, 98.0, 96.3, 85.0, 99.0 (Table 5). The judge is an LLM, with no inter-rater or human comparison reported.

HOW ENVIRONMENTS ARE GENERATED AND VERIFIED (note 06 and note 07)
- Six stages (Fig 1, p3): seed, tools and corpus; blueprint initialization (scenario, persona, parameters); blueprint construction; maze materialization; ground truth and verifier assembly; evaluation and failure analysis.
- The blueprint fixes the solution space, environment requirements and verification criteria before any environment exists. A reconciliation check confirms that omitted values stay discoverable in the environment and that the tools support a solution.
- Answerability invariant: ground truth is computed by executing the blueprint's solution derivation against the materialized environment, not taken from values the generator proposed (p5). A separate pass checks that the derivation uses authoritative resources, is unaffected by distractors and admits no equally defensible alternative.
- Verifier has four signals: outcome correctness, process quality, distractor resilience and personalization. Programmatic rules cover deterministic outcomes and distractors. A three-stage judge pipeline (process judge, outcome judge, meta-judge) scores open-ended outcomes and process. The meta-judge outputs a reward in [0,1] and a root-cause class (pass, environment failure, ambiguous, agent error). Strong process with a correct outcome scores highest; a correct outcome with weak process is discounted; correct process with a wrong outcome gets partial credit (App C, p17).
- Difficulty parameters (App A): three topology tiers (retrieval, multi-hop/multi-constraint/list aggregation, cross-source comparison); 7 capability axes, each with a validation predicate (for example, matches must exceed page size for exhaustive aggregation); obfuscation gradient 0.0-1.0; distractor budget over persona, content and tool channels. C1 and C2 differ only in tier weights (Tier 1/2/3 0.5/0.3/0.2 against 0.1/0.4/0.5), obfuscation (0.0-0.5 against 0.3-1.0) and distractors per task (3-5 against 3-10) (p16).
- Curriculum rule (p6): sampling weights are adjusted when capability-dimension success is below 0.30 (relaxed) or above 0.80 (strengthened), with bounded updates.
- Human validation: inspectors checked reachability, that no distractor blocks all routes, and that the verifier matches the task intent. This was done on all retained tasks (p8).
- Substrate: relational store with tool wrappers. Appendix E gives a cloud-API emulator example using a declarative state definition with a _ground_truth annotation; it is not evaluated empirically.

LIMITS
- Only two evaluated settings (productivity, temporal), with two models (Opus 4.6, gpt-oss-120b). No seeds or confidence intervals are reported; eight rollouts per task.
- The generator is Sonnet 4.6, from the same family as the frontier reference, Opus 4.6.
- Difficulty is judged against the evaluated model only. There is no ablation of blueprint-first against single-pass generation within AutoGym; the comparison is to AWM and human tasks, which differ in other ways. The AWM baseline was manually filtered. The curriculum loop is shown for one round, with no multi-round convergence plot.
- Authors concede: interface realism is weakest (78.0) and distractors are unnaturally integrated; open-ended tasks still rely partly on LLM judgment; the RL test is one 8B model, 500 steps; the cloud substrate is unevaluated (p9).
- The paper does not show that training on these gyms improves held-out agent skill.
- Amazon AGI authors, no code link seen.

BUILDS ON: Agent World Model (Wang et al., 2026) as the direct inspiration and baseline; AgentGen (Hu et al., 2024); EnvScaler (Song et al., 2025); tau2-bench programmatic assertions (Barres et al., 2025); SWE-Gym (Pan et al., 2025); WebRL (Qi et al., 2024); APIGen (Liu et al., 2024b); Lightman et al. 2024 process supervision; Zheng et al. 2023 LLM-judge bias; DeepSeek-R1 and Tülu 3 for verifiable-reward RL.

CODE: none beyond a declarative JSON state with _ground_truth annotations (p20-21) and prompt templates (App H, p22-28).

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p3) shows the six-stage pipeline in one view. Fig 2 (p22) shows training reward over 500 GRPO steps, with no numbers.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean apart from spaced-out JSON on p20 and merged words (e.g. "agym"). The text/table mismatch of 89.1% against 89.2% is noted above. I did not fully read pages 24-28 (verifier prompt templates), only their start.
